 by CORY SMITH | The National News Desk

 (TNND) — Early voting is up this year, with stronger Democratic participation that lines up with their enthusiasm advantage seen in poll after poll.
 An early-voting tracker run by political scientist Michael McDonald at the University of Florida showed over 30 million ballots had been cast as of Monday afternoon.
 With just over a week to go until Election Day, 45% of the early vote had come from Democrats, compared to around 30% from Republicans and around a quarter from unaffiliated voters or voters affiliated with another party. That’s based on party registration data available from over two dozen states.
 That shows who has already voted but not how they voted.
 McDonald said he’s seeing consistent partisan breakdowns across states.
 Democrats and unaffiliated voters are generally casting early votes at a faster pace than they did in the last midterm election in 2022.
 Meanwhile, he said Republicans have not kept pace with their 2022 numbers in some states.
 And McDonald said the early-voting figures support the outlook that Democrats are set up for a strong midterm election “from a holistic standpoint.”
 Polling from the Pew Research Center , AP-NORC , KFF , Marquette Law School and others show Democrats are voicing higher motivation to vote than Republicans. McDonald said the early-voting participation is consistent with that polling.
 McDonald said neither economic sentiment nor President Donald Trump’s approval rating favors Republicans. And he said that’s showing up in where the two sides are choosing to spend their money and send their surrogates to campaign.
 Everything is consistently indicating that “the Democrats are going to be competitive in some places that they haven't been recently competitive, and that could tip the U.S. Senate,” McDonald said.
 The president’s party historically loses seats in most midterm elections. The sitting president’s party has lost House seats in eight of 10 midterms going back 40 years. The same has happened six times over that span in the Senate.
 “Most likely the Democrats will gain control of the U.S. House,” McDonald continued. “I think that's pretty much a done deal now, because of how the Republicans are playing defense.”
 Rice University political scientist Mark Jones said control of the Senate, meanwhile, will be determined by what voters decide in a handful of states. Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas appear to be the most competitive .
 “But it could, possibly, be that until Election Day, we really don't know if this is just a bad election for Republicans or a cataclysmic election for Republicans,” Jones said.
 Jones cautioned against reading too much into early-voting figures, though he, too, said the early-voting trend is in line with other indicators of a strong year for Democrats.
 “If you're a Democrat, you have more reasons to be optimistic than Republicans,” Jones said. “Democrats know their voters are turning out in large numbers, and many of them have already cast a ballot. Republicans have to hope that their voters who have not yet turned out to vote actually do turn out, either during the final week of early voting in most states or on Election Day. So, it's just like in football, where you definitely feel better if it's the fourth quarter, you have a touchdown lead, and you have the ball. That doesn't mean you're going to win, but you're feeling good about it.”
 Jones said turnout is likely to exceed an average midterm election, coming closer to “presidential-level election turnout.”
 SEE ALSO: Economic gloom could spell political doom for Republicans in next month's midterms 
 DES MOINES, IOWA - OCTOBER 14: Voters fill out their ballots during early voting at the Polk County Election Office on October 14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa. Wednesday was the first day Iowans could cast an early in-person ballot in the general election.(Photo by Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images) 
 Sure enough, McDonald said early voting is outpacing 2022 levels.
 Pennsylvania and Tennessee are exceptions, he said.
 “Every other state where I've done this analysis, it's pacing ahead,” McDonald said.
 Early voting is setting the stage for a “fairly robust turnout” this election, McDonald said.
 “Hard to say exactly where we're going to land right now, but it is very possible that we will have a higher turnout rate than 2018. That was the highest turnout rate for a midterm election since 1914,” he said.
 Of the 30 million or so early ballots that had been cast as of Monday afternoon, roughly half were in person and roughly half were sent in by mail.
 Nearly 60 million mail ballots have been requested, of which nearly 15 million, or about a quarter, have already been returned, according to McDonald’s tracking.
 McDonald said his analysis shows people are returning ballots sooner in the states where they can only vote early by mail. He said there might be some concern among voters about their ballots getting back to election offices in time.
 He said where voters can choose between mail and in-person early voting, more people are opting to vote in person.
 He also said the early-voting data is “clearly showing” that Hispanics are “voting at unprecedented numbers.” McDonald is also seeing higher levels of early-voting participation by Black voters in the handful of states that report race and ethnicity data from voter registration.
 McDonald said a more diverse electorate seems to be shaping up for this election – another signal that favors Democrats.
